passage: Preeti, you're moving into the hostel next week, so let your Vijay Mama tell you about his first flat in Pune. I shared it with a boy called Mohan. One morning I found a note on the fridge: "Wow, you washed a plate! Should we call the newspapers?" Then another: "Thank you SO much for leaving your socks on the sofa. Very decorative." Every note made my ears go hot. I felt attacked, and I couldn't even argue with a fridge. So I started leaving notes back, sharper ones. Two weeks of paper war. Then my mother said on the phone, "Vijay, ask him what he actually wants." So I did, one evening over chai. Mohan said he was tired of doing the dishes alone. We made a rota. No more notes. So, Preeti, if someone starts writing you notes, go and have chai with them.

qa.q: What did the first note on the fridge say?
qa.a: "Wow, you washed a plate! Should we call the newspapers?"

qa.q: Why did the notes make Vijay's ears go hot?
qa.a: He felt attacked and mocked, with no fair chance to reply, since he couldn't argue with a fridge.

qa.q: What turning point ended the paper war?
qa.a: Following his mother's advice to ask Mohan what he actually wanted, over chai, which led to a dish rota.

qa.q: What might Mohan have been feeling when he wrote the notes?
qa.a: Tired and resentful about doing the dishes alone, but unable or unwilling to say so directly.

grounding: An uncle recalls how a flatmate's sarcastic notes left him feeling attacked until he calmly asked what the flatmate wanted to change.

passage:
It was exam week, the water in their building came for only two hours a day, and Karthik had a thermodynamics paper at nine. At 6 a.m. he found a sticky note on the kettle in Sabina's handwriting: "Thanks SO much for washing your mug. For once. Truly a miracle." Another was stuck to the bucket: "Love how the water fills itself."
Karthik's face burned. He had been up till two studying. He wanted to write something vicious on the back. Instead, before the water came on, he knocked on her door. "Sabina, I saw the notes. I don't want a war before exams. What's bothering you? What do you want me to change?"
She blinked, then sighed. "I've been filling the buckets alone every morning. I'm exhausted too."
They split the mornings: he would take Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

qa.q: What did the note on the kettle say?
qa.a: "Thanks SO much for washing your mug. For once. Truly a miracle."

qa.q: Why did Karthik's face burn when he read the notes?
qa.a: He felt attacked while already exhausted from studying, and a note gave him no fair chance to answer.

qa.q: What choice did Karthik make instead of writing something vicious, and why did it work?
qa.a: He knocked and calmly asked what was bothering Sabina and what she wanted changed, which uncovered the real problem of filling buckets alone. 👍

qa.q: What was the week like for Sabina before Karthik knocked?
qa.a: Exhausting, filling the buckets alone every morning during exams, with resentment building until it leaked out in sarcastic notes.

grounding: During exam week and a water shortage a student finds sarcastic notes from his flatmate, feels attacked, and calmly asks what she wants changed.

passage:
Gargi came back from the library to find a note on her pillow in their PG room in Mukherjee Nagar: "Thanks for the lovely music at 1 a.m.! I didn't need sleep anyway 🙂" The next day there was one on the mirror: "So kind of you to leave your hair in the sink. A gift!"
Gargi stared at the neat handwriting. Neelam, her roommate, was at her desk with headphones on, not looking up. Gargi's chest tightened. She wanted to rip the note off and say something clever and cutting. She had no idea how long Neelam had been angry.
That evening, when Neelam took off her headphones, Gargi said, "I found the notes. I'd rather hear it straight. What would you like me to change?"
Neelam went red. "The music at night, mostly. I have an early coaching class."
Gargi nodded. "Headphones after eleven. And I'll clear the sink. Deal?"

qa.q: Where did Gargi find the second note?
qa.a: On the mirror.

qa.q: Why did Gargi's chest tighten when she saw Neelam with headphones on?
qa.a: She felt attacked by the notes and shut out, with no idea how long Neelam had been angry and no fair chance to reply.

qa.q: Which choice turned the note war into a solution?
qa.a: Asking Neelam calmly what she would like changed, which brought out the real problem of late music and led to a clear deal.

qa.q: Why might Neelam have written notes instead of speaking up?
qa.a: She may have felt awkward confronting Gargi directly, so the irritation came out sideways as sarcasm.

grounding: A student finds sarcastic 'thank you' notes from her roommate, feels attacked without a chance to reply, and calmly asks what the roommate wants.

passage:
"Sunaina, got a minute?"
"Sure." She didn't look up from her laptop.
"I found this on the fridge." Vikas held up the sticky note. "'Dear Vikas, the pans say thank you for finally meeting you.' And yesterday's, on the kettle."
"Just a joke."
"It didn't feel like one. It felt like being told off, with no way to answer." He sat on the arm of the sofa in their shared flat. "I'd rather hear it straight. What do you want me to change?"
She closed the laptop. "...Honestly? The pans sitting overnight. I cook at seven and there's nothing clean."
"Okay. That's fair. What if I wash up before I sleep, every night?"
"And no more notes?"
"No more notes. Just tell me."
She peeled the note off his hand and crumpled it. "Deal. Sorry. The notes were easier than saying it."

qa.q: What did the note on the fridge say?
qa.a: "Dear Vikas, the pans say thank you for finally meeting you."

qa.q: How did the notes make Vikas feel?
qa.a: Attacked and told off, with no fair way to answer 😔, which is why he didn't find them funny.

qa.q: What did Vikas's calm question change?
qa.a: Asking "What do you want me to change?" turned the sarcasm into a clear request about the overnight pans and a plan to wash up before sleeping.

qa.q: Why might Sunaina have written notes instead of saying it?
qa.a: She admits the notes were easier than saying it; speaking directly may have felt awkward, so the frustration came out as jokes.

grounding: Shows a student who feels attacked by a flatmate's sarcastic thank-you notes and calmly asks what she wants changed, which turns the notes into a clear request.

passage:
Looking back at my first year, the notes were the worst part. My cousin Mahima and I shared a small flat near college, and I was, I admit, not a great dishwasher. But I didn't know she minded until the notes started. "Congratulations on washing ONE spoon! A historic day." Then: "The sink would like to meet you sometime. It's heard so much about you."
I felt ambushed every time I walked into the kitchen. You can't argue with a sticky note. I started coming home late just to avoid them.
Then one evening, instead of writing back something nasty, which I'd already drafted, I knocked on her door. "Mahima, I'm getting the notes. I think you're really fed up. What exactly do you want me to change?"
She went quiet, then said, "Wash up the same night. That's it." We made a rota on an actual piece of paper. Now she calls me "Deepak the Dishwasher", but to my face, and I laugh.

qa.q: What did the second note say about the sink?
qa.a: "The sink would like to meet you sometime. It's heard so much about you."

qa.q: Why did Deepak start coming home late?
qa.a: Deepak felt ambushed and on edge because of notes that couldn't be answered, so avoiding the kitchen seemed easier than facing them.

qa.q: What turning point ended the notes?
qa.a: Deepak knocked instead of sending the nasty reply and calmly asked what Mahima wanted changed, which led to a clear answer and a rota.

qa.q: What might Mahima have been feeling before Deepak knocked?
qa.a: Mahima was likely fed up and resentful about the dishes, but found it easier to hide the anger in sarcastic notes than to say it directly.

grounding: Illustrates a student who feels ambushed by a flatmate's sarcastic notes and finds a way out by calmly asking what she wants to change.
